title: Assignment 1 - EPPS 6356
text:
In his paper (1973), Anscombe claims that visualizing data is crucial for statistical analysis. To support his claim, he presented a dataset that generated four different visualizations in which the data displays totally different behaviors, even though the regression summary was exactly the same for all. That illustrates the fact that only by running statistical/mathematical metrics may not be enough for a scientist to understand the underlying nature of data.
In his paper, Anscombe suggested that data that is not linear could be adjusted by applying transformation functions to the x-axis, to the y-axis or both. Today, with libraries such as the scikit-learn library in Python, it is possible to conduct multiple types of transformations not only to linearize data but also to shape the data under several desired statistical distributions.
Thus, using Python is a possible and efficient method I would suggest to go around problems associated with nonlinear data, as addressed by Anscombe.

## Data Visualization
## Objective: Create graphics with R
## Title: Fall color
# Credit: https://fronkonstin.com

# Install packages
#install.packages(c("gsubfn", "proto", "tidyverse"))

library(gsubfn)
library(tidyverse)

# Define elements in plant art
# Each image corresponds to a different axiom, rules, angle and depth

# Leaf of Fall

axiom="X"
rules=list("X"="F-[[X]+X]+F[+FX]-X", "F"="FF")
angle=22.5
depth=6


for (i in 1:depth) axiom=gsubfn(".", rules, axiom)

actions=str_extract_all(axiom, "\\d*\\+|\\d*\\-|F|L|R|\\[|\\]|\\|") %>% unlist

status=data.frame(x=numeric(0), y=numeric(0), alfa=numeric(0))
points=data.frame(x1 = 0, y1 = 0, x2 = NA, y2 = NA, alfa=90, depth=1)


# Generating data
# Note: may take a minute or two

for (action in actions)
{
  if (action=="F")
  {
    x=points[1, "x1"]+cos(points[1, "alfa"]*(pi/180))
    y=points[1, "y1"]+sin(points[1, "alfa"]*(pi/180))
    points[1,"x2"]=x
    points[1,"y2"]=y
    data.frame(x1 = x, y1 = y, x2 = NA, y2 = NA,
               alfa=points[1, "alfa"],
               depth=points[1,"depth"]) %>% rbind(points)->points
  }
  if (action %in% c("+", "-")){
    alfa=points[1, "alfa"]
    points[1, "alfa"]=eval(parse(text=paste0("alfa",action, angle)))
  }
  if(action=="["){
    data.frame(x=points[1, "x1"], y=points[1, "y1"], alfa=points[1, "alfa"]) %>%
      rbind(status) -> status
    points[1, "depth"]=points[1, "depth"]+1
  }
  
  if(action=="]"){
    depth=points[1, "depth"]
    points[-1,]->points
    data.frame(x1=status[1, "x"], y1=status[1, "y"], x2=NA, y2=NA,
               alfa=status[1, "alfa"],
               depth=depth-1) %>%
      rbind(points) -> points
    status[-1,]->status
  }
}

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2),
               lineend = "round",
               color="tomato", # Set your own Fall: "tomato"
               data=na.omit(points)) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1) +
  theme_void() # No grid nor axes












*Write a critique on a chart in published work (book/article/news website)
The following chart was collected from https://viz.wtf/ and reprdduces a chart published by The New York Times.
The graph is a total mess. First, the timeline is represented as a spiral, which is not natural for humans. A straight timeline on the x-axis, in ascending order would be much more intuitive. Also, the intervals are confusing. The graph shows years, months and days on the same timeline, making it hard to distinguish what the metrics are effectivelly attempting to communicate. The numeric legend is also confusing. The user does not know immediately if the legend intends to be read as a color or as a triangular shape.

title: Assignment 02 - EPPS 6302
text:
This assignment addresses term searches on Google Trends

The following notes reproduce the scripts used for each search, an overview of the scraped data and the respective plots.





library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)
library(DT)








Terms: Trump, Harris, election
Countries: United States
Group: Web
Time window: Last 5 years
Category: All categories (news, youtube, images etc)


TrumpHarrisElection = gtrends(c("Trump","Harris","election"), 
                              onlyInterest = TRUE, 
                              geo = "US", 
                              gprop = "web", 
                              time = "today+5-y", # last five years
                              category = 0 
) 
df=TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time
plot(TrumpHarrisElection)







DT::datatable(TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time)













Terms: immigration
Countries: all
Group: alll
Time window: alll
Category: all


query2 <- gtrends("immigration", time = "all")
plot(query2)







DT::datatable(query2$interest_over_time)













Terms: immigration
Countries: United States, Great Britain, Taiwan
Group: alll
Time window: alll
Category: all


query3 <- gtrends("immigration", geo = c("US", "GB", "TW"), time = "all")
plot(query3)







DT::datatable(query3$interest_over_time)

title: John Vasconcelos
text: I am a PhD student in Public and Nonprofit Management at the University of Texas at Dallas. My research interests cover topics associated with public financial and performance accountability oversight, such as public sector auditing and financial compliance, utilizing advanced statistics and artificial intelligence.

title: Research
text:
Machine Learning applied to Public Sector Auditing: A case study with data from the department of health of the state of São Paulo, Brazil

Abstract:
Machine Learning (ML), as a field of Artificial Intelligence (AI), has become increasingly popular due to its ease of learning, scalability, and low cost. Both industry and academia have researched useful and feasible ways to apply ML algorithms for practical use in multiple fields, both academic and professional, taking advantage of their ability to learn patterns to predict future variables, classify or group data, and detect anomalous observations. Although the private sector has quickly evolved in studying the application of ML to financial fraud, stock market modeling and financial distress prediction, the application of these techniques in the public sector, namely in public audit, still demands further research for practical use. In this paper, I conduct a review of the current literature on machine learning applications for management-related fields and propose a case study to advance its application to public audit. I identified the Isolation Forest (iForest) algorithm as one of the most effective, scalable, and recognized for detecting anomalies. I applied it to a dataset with expenditure data from the Department of Health of the city of São Paulo, Brazil, and found that the algorithm can be of practical use for anomalous transaction value detection, but ineffective in identifying expenditure misclassification. The paper contributes to the scarce literature on the application of ML to public audit and seeks to promote further investigation for public oversight and improved management.
